answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1873–1947 · American novelist of the Great Plains
answer.sourceLine: From her 1918 novel My Ántonia, Book I, Chapter II — the boy Jim Burden, drowsing in his grandmother’s garden. The line is genuine and confirmed against the primary text; the original wording is “At any rate, that is happiness; to be dissolved into something complete and great” (a semicolon, not the colon often seen).

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: I was something that lay under the sun and felt it, like the pumpkins, and I did not want to be anything more. I was entirely happy. Perhaps we feel like that when we die and become a part of something entire, whether it is sun and air, or goodness and knowledge. At any rate, that is happiness; to be dissolved into something complete and great. When it comes to one, it comes as naturally as sleep.
trail: The exact sentence sits in Book I, Chapter II of My Ántonia (1918), confirmed against Project Gutenberg’s full text.
Wikiquote lists it in its sourced section, citing My Ántonia, Book I, Ch. 2.
Cather chose a fragment of the line for her own gravestone inscription.
source.excerptNote: The popular short form drops the opening “At any rate,” and often swaps the original semicolon for a colon.

author.name: Willa Cather
author.heading: About Willa Cather
author.bio: Willa Cather (1873–1947) was an American writer celebrated for her novels of frontier and immigrant life on the Great Plains, among them O Pioneers!, The Song of the Lark and My Ántonia. She won the 1923 Pulitzer Prize for One of Ours. She held this passage close enough that a fragment of it is carved on her gravestone in Jaffrey, New Hampshire.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The attribution here is right — this really is Willa Cather. What travels in a slightly altered form is the wording.

items.why: The line is endlessly reproduced with a colon — “That is happiness: to be dissolved…” — but Cather’s original uses a semicolon: “that is happiness; to be dissolved into something complete and great,” per the 1918 text.
The sentence actually opens “At any rate, that is happiness…” — the hedging phrase is almost always cut when the line is quoted alone.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Cather’s, from My Ántonia (1918), Book I, Ch. II — just usually re-punctuated and trimmed of its “At any rate,” opening (Wikiquote, sourced).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line comes from one of the quietest moments in My Ántonia: the orphaned boy Jim Burden, newly arrived in Nebraska, lies alone in his grandmother’s pumpkin patch and feels himself dissolve into the warm earth and sun. It is a meditation on happiness as self-forgetting — becoming “a part of something entire.”
Cather held the passage close enough to make it her epitaph: a fragment is carved on her headstone in the Old Burying Ground at Jaffrey, New Hampshire.
